claims.disproof_condition: Downgrade if future USGS MCS editions show materially diversified US import sources (China share well below 50%) or effective substitutes reaching commercial adoption in magnet applications.
claims.statement: USGS 2026: US rare-earth compound/metal imports came 71% from China (2021-24); substitutes for rare earths are available for many applications but generally less effective; China imposed export controls on key magnet elements (Tb, Dy, Sm, Gd) in April 2025. This is the structural backdrop that makes non-China rare-earth supply relationships hard to substitute.

source_doc.origin_entity: U.S. Geological Survey (美國政府第三方統計，非任何生產商)
source_doc.title: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 — Rare Earths

sources.quote: Bastnaesite was mined as a primary product in Mountain Pass, CA.
Rare-earth compounds and metals: China, 71%; Malaysia, 13%; Japan, 5%; Estonia, 5%; and other, 6%.
Substitutes are available for many applications but generally are less effective.

In April 2025, China tightened its export controls on rare-earth elements, adding specific controls on alloys, compounds, metals, and oxides of samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium.
